title: Last weekend and what's next
goal: Wrap up level A1: the other side of the past tense, which uses *essere* and changes form, and how to talk about plans without the future tense at all.
bekal: make the past participle agree when using *essere*
talk about plans with the present tense and *andare a*

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Com'è andato il fine settimana?
dialogs.intro: The last unit. Count how many times *sono* appears and how many times *ho* — and watch the last letter of the word that follows.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Giulia, com'è andato il fine settimana?
lines.literal: Giulia, how-is gone the end week?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Benissimo. Sono andata a Firenze con mia sorella.
lines.id: Great. I went to Florence with my sister.
lines.literal: very-well. I-am gone(f) to Florence with my sister.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Sabato mattina presto. Siamo arrivate alle nove.
lines.id: Early Saturday morning. We got there at nine.
lines.literal: saturday morning early. we-are arrived(f-pl) at-the nine.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Abbiamo visitato gli Uffizi e abbiamo camminato tutto il giorno.
lines.id: We visited the Uffizi and walked all day.
lines.literal: we-have visited the Uffizi and we-have walked all the day.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Sì, una notte. Siamo tornate domenica sera, stanchissime.
lines.id: Yes, one night. We came back Sunday evening, exhausted.
lines.literal: yes, one night. we-are returned(f-pl) sunday evening, very-tired(f-pl).

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Io invece sono rimasto a casa. Ho lavorato tutto il weekend.
lines.id: I just stayed home. I worked all weekend.
lines.literal: I instead am stayed(m) at home. I-have worked all the weekend.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Poverino. E il prossimo fine settimana che fai?
lines.id: Poor thing. And what are you doing next weekend?
lines.literal: poor-little-one. and the next end week what you-do?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Niente lavoro. Vado al mare e non porto il telefono.
lines.id: No work. I'm going to the beach and I'm not taking my phone.
lines.literal: no work. I-go to-the sea and not I-bring the phone.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Bravo! Allora buon riposo — e buon proseguimento con l'italiano, Budi!
lines.id: Good for you! Have a good rest, then — and keep going with your Italian, Budi!
lines.literal: well-done! then good rest — and good continuation with the italian, Budi!

notes: **A group of verbs uses essere, not avere.** Most of them express movement or a change of state: go, come, arrive, leave, enter, go out, go up, go down, stay, be born, die, become.
**And with essere, the past participle changes form.** *Sono andato* (a man), *sono andata* (a woman), *siamo andati* (a group), *siamo andate* (an all-female group). Exactly like a normal adjective.
**With avere it never changes.** *Ho mangiato* sounds the same whoever says it. That's the practical reason choosing the right helper verb matters: it decides whether the last letter changes.
**How to remember it.** Verbs that take an object use *avere*: eat **what**, read **what**, see **whom**. Verbs with no object that express movement use *essere*: go, come, arrive.
**All reflexive verbs use essere.** *Mi sono alzato*, *ci siamo svegliati*, *si è vestita*. No exceptions — which saves a lot of hesitation.

**Italian hardly uses the future tense for plans.** *Domani vado al mare*, *l'anno prossimo torno in Indonesia* — the present tense plus a time word, much like English "I'm going to the beach tomorrow". The real future tense exists, but it's used more for predictions and guesses, and that's B1 territory.

**Poverino** = "poor thing", literally "poor little one". The feminine is *poverina*. The ending *-ino* adds a sense of smallness or affection to almost any word: *un caffettino*, *un momentino*, *una casina*.
**Buon proseguimento** is the Italian wish for something still under way — a trip, a meal, your studies. A fitting send-off for this module.

grammars.title: Verbs that use essere
body: The A1 list is short and closed. Learn all of it; outside this list, almost everything uses *avere*.
after: Notice that *essere* and *stare* share the same past form: *stato*. *Sono stato a Roma* means "I've been to Rome" — the most common way to talk about experiences.
*Piacere* also uses *essere*, and it's still backwards: *mi è piaciuto il film*, *mi sono piaciute le lasagne*. The thing liked decides the form.

grammars.title: Making the last letter agree
body: Exactly like an adjective of the *-o* group.

head: Who
Ending
Example
rows: Giulia e sua sorella sono andat**e**.

after: ⚠️ The most common mistake for English speakers: using *-o* for everyone, because English never marks gender on verbs. A woman saying *sono andato* sounds wrong right away — just as much as a man saying *sono andata*.

grammars.title: Talking about plans

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: I'm going to the beach tomorrow.
I'm thinking of leaving on Monday.

after: The first two patterns cover nearly all everyday conversation. The last two sound a bit more formal and are useful in writing.

sections.title: Telling the story of a weekend

blocks.text: Everything you need to tell the story of two days, put together in one example. Read it out loud, then swap in your own weekend.

blocks.title: Sample story
items: *Sabato mi sono alzata tardi e ho fatto colazione a casa.*
*Poi sono uscita e sono andata al mercato con un'amica.*
*Abbiamo comprato del pane, della frutta e un po' di formaggio.*
*A mezzogiorno abbiamo pranzato in una trattoria vicino alla piazza.*
*Nel pomeriggio ho letto un libro al parco. Faceva bel tempo.*
*La sera sono rimasta a casa e ho visto un film.*
*Domenica sono partita presto per Firenze e sono tornata alle otto.*

blocks.text: Notice the switching: *sono alzata*, *sono uscita*, *sono andata*, *sono rimasta*, *sono partita*, *sono tornata* all use *essere* and end in *-a* because the speaker is a woman; while *ho fatto*, *abbiamo comprato*, *abbiamo pranzato*, *ho letto*, *ho visto* use *avere* and don't change at all.

blocks.title: Common wrap-up phrases
items: *Mi sono divertito / divertita molto.* — I had a great time.
*Non ho fatto niente di speciale.* — I didn't do anything special.
*È stata una settimana lunga.* — It's been a long week.

blocks.text: These twenty units cover all of Level A1. You can now introduce yourself, ask and answer questions about people and places, order food, go shopping, tell the time and the date, ask for directions, say what you like and don't like, ask permission, and talk about what has happened and what you're going to do. That's no small thing.

Not yet in this module, and waiting at the next level: the past tense for habits (*imperfetto*), the real future tense, object pronouns (*lo*, *la*, *li*, *le*, *ne*), and the conditional. All of them run on the engine you installed in unit 6 and unit 19.
One last piece of advice. Don't wait until you feel ready to speak — that feeling never comes. Find someone to talk to now, with the hundred words you already have. *In bocca al lupo!*

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct form of essere or avere.
Make the last letter of the past participle agree.
items: Le mie sorelle sono partit__ ieri.
Marco e Giulia sono arrivat__ insieme.
On Saturday I went to Florence.
I came back on Sunday evening.
Next weekend I'm going to the beach.
I intend to study Italian next year.

answers: sono — ha — è — abbiamo — sono — Ho
andata — tornato — partite — arrivati — rimasta — usciti
Sono andato al mare. — Mi sono alzato alle sette. — Marco è uscito di casa. — Siamo tornati a mezzanotte. — Giulia è rimasta a Firenze. — I miei amici sono arrivati tardi.

Sabato sono andato a Firenze. — Siamo arrivati alle nove. — Abbiamo visitato il museo. — Sono tornato domenica sera. — Il prossimo fine settimana vado al mare. — Ho intenzione di studiare l'italiano l'anno prossimo.
